Surah al-Fil is Meccan. [Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "(Have you not seen) was revealed in Mecca." See al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/627.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

The story of the companions of the elephant, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq from some of the people of knowledge, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and as also mentioned by al-Waqidi, is as follows:

The Negus, king of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), had sent Aryat to the land of Yemen, and he gained control of it. Then a man from Abyssinia, called Abraha ibn al-Sabah [Abu Yaksum] (the words in brackets are an addition from manuscript "A"), rose against Aryat over the affair of the Abyssinians, until they split into two factions. One group was with Aryat and another with Abraha. They clashed, and Abraha killed Aryat. The Abyssinians gathered around Abraha, he gained control of Yemen, and the Negus confirmed him in his post.

Then Abraha saw people preparing during the days of the season (al-mawsim) to travel to Mecca for the Pilgrimage to the House of Allah. So he built a church (kanisah) in Sanaa and wrote to the Negus: "I have built for you in Sanaa a church the like of which has not been built for any king, and I will not desist until I divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it." A man from the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah heard of this (he went there secretly, the words in brackets being an addition from manuscript "B"), entered it at night, sat in it, defecated in it, and smeared its qibla with filth. When this reached Abraha, he said: "Who has dared to act against me and smear my church with filth?" He was told: "A man from the Arabs, from the people of that House, did that, having heard what you said." Abraha swore at that moment: "I will surely march on the Kaʿbah until I demolish it." He wrote to the Negus informing him of this and asking him to send him his elephant. He had an elephant called Mahmud, which was unmatched in size, bulk and strength. So it was sent to him. Abraha set out from Abyssinia toward Mecca, and the elephant went with him. When the Arabs heard of this, they were greatly alarmed and considered fighting him a duty upon them. A king of the kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafar, went out with those of his people who obeyed him, fought him, and Abraha defeated him and took Dhu Nafar. Dhu Nafar said: "O king, do not kill me, for sparing me is better for you than killing me." So he spared him and bound him. Abraha was a forbearing man.

Then he marched on until, when he approached the lands of Khathʿam, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khathʿami went out with Khathʿam and those who had gathered to him from the tribes of Yemen. They fought him, and he defeated them and took Nufayl. Nufayl said: "O king, I am a guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are upon my people in hearing and obedience." So he spared him, and Nufayl went with him as a guide. When he passed by al-Taʾif, Masʿud ibn Muʿattib came out to him with men of Thaqif and said: "O king, we are your slaves; there is no opposition to you from us. You only want the House in Mecca; we will send with you someone to guide you to it." So they sent with him Abu Righal, a client of theirs. He set out until, when he was at al-Mughammas (a place near Mecca on the road to al-Taʾif; see Muʿjam al-Buldan), Abu Righal died. He is the one whose grave is stoned. Then Abraha sent from al-Mughammas a man from Abyssinia called al-Aswad ibn Masʿud at the head of his cavalry, and ordered him to raid the camels of the people. al-Aswad gathered the wealth of the Haram to himself and seized two hundred camels belonging to ʿAbd al-Muttalib.

Then Abraha sent Hanatah al-Himyari to the people of Mecca, saying: "Ask about their chief, then convey to him what I have sent you with. Tell him that I have not come to fight; I have only come to demolish this House." So he set out until he entered Mecca and met ʿAbd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim. He said: "The king has sent me to you to tell you that he has not come to fight, unless you fight him. He has only come to demolish this House, and then to depart from you."

ʿAbd al-Muttalib said: "We have no fight with him, nor any power against him, except that we leave between him and what he came for. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the House of His friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him. If He prevents him from it, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves him between it and that, then by Allah we have no strength against him."

[Hanatah] said: "Then go with me to the king." It is reported by some scholars that he rode him on a mule he had, and some of his sons rode with him, until he arrived at the army encampment. Dhu Nafar was a friend of ʿAbd al-Muttalib, so he came to him and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any help in what has befallen us?" He said: "What help can a captive man give, who does not feel safe from being killed at morning or evening? But I will send to Unays, the elephant keeper, for he is my friend, and ask him to do for you with the king whatever good he can, and to enhance your standing and rank with him." He said: So he sent for Unays, who came to him, and he said to him: "This is the chief of Quraysh, the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. The king has seized two hundred camels from him. If you can benefit him with him, then do so, for he is my friend; I love for him whatever good reaches him."

So Unays entered upon Abraha and said: "O king, this is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. He asks permission to come to you, and I love that you permit him so that he may speak with you. He has come neither hostile to you nor opposing you." So he gave him permission.

ʿAbd al-Muttalib was a tall, handsome man. When Abraha saw him, he esteemed and honored him, and he disliked that he should sit with him on the throne while he sat beneath him. So he came down onto the carpet and sat upon it, then called him and seated him beside himself. Then he said to his interpreter: "Tell him: what is your need of the king?" The interpreter said that to him. ʿAbd al-Muttalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me the two hundred camels he seized from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you." ʿAbd al-Muttalib said: "Why?" He said: "I came to a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and which is your honor and your protection, in order to demolish it, and you did not speak to me about it, but you speak to me about two hundred camels I have taken?" ʿAbd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of these camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He could not prevent me from it." He said: "Then that is your affair." So he ordered his camels to be returned to him.

When the camels were returned to ʿAbd al-Muttalib, he went out and informed Quraysh of the matter, and ordered them to scatter in the ravines and take refuge on the mountain tops, out of fear for them from the harm of the army. They did so. ʿAbd al-Muttalib went to the Kaʿbah, took hold of the ring of its door, and began to say:

"O Lord, I hope for none but You to protect them.
O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Surely the enemy of the House is the enemy of You;
Keep them from ruining Your sacred place."

He also said: "O Allah [Lahumma; its original form is Allahumma, and the Arabs drop the alif and lam from it and suffice with what remains; they say lah abuka, meaning Allah's father], surely a servant defends his household, so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their might prevail over Your might tomorrow [ghadwan: ghada, the day that comes after your day, its final letter dropped, and it is not used in full except in poetry; mihal: strength and force].
They have marched the hosts of their lands and the elephant, that they may take captive Your dependants.
They have assailed Your sanctuary with their scheming, in ignorance, and they did not regard Your majesty.
If You leave them and our Kaʿbah, then it is Your affair."

"I have never heard of more abject men than those who wished to raid, to violate Your sacred things." [This verse is an addition from manuscript "A".]

Then ʿAbd al-Muttalib left the ring and set off with his people in some of those directions. Abraha had prepared to enter, arranged his army and readied his elephant at al-Mughammas at dawn. It was an elephant the like of which had not been seen for size and strength. It is said that twelve elephants were with him.

Nufayl approached the greatest elephant, took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return in peace from where you came, for you are in the land of Allah, the Sacred." The elephant knelt. They urged it to rise, but it refused. They struck it on the head with an iron hook, but it refused. They put their hooks under its belly and its shoulders and pulled it so that it would stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it rose and ran at a trot. They turned it toward Syria, and it did the same. They turned it toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward the Haram, and it knelt down and refused to rise.

Nufayl went off running until he climbed up the mountain. Allah sent against them birds from the sea, like swallows, each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet and one in its beak, the size of chickpeas and lentils. When they came over the people, they released them upon them, and those stones did not strike anyone without his being destroyed. Not all of the people were struck, and they fled, not finding the way they had come by, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Nufayl was looking at them from some of those mountains. The people cried out, and some of them surged over others, falling down along every path and perishing at every place of destruction.

Allah sent upon Abraha an ailment in his body, so that his fingertips began to fall off. Whenever a fingertip fell, a discharge of pus and blood followed it (the thick part is pus; the thin part is ichor). He reached Sanaa like a baby bird, along with those of his companions who remained, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart, and then he perished. [Ibn Hisham related this: 1/44–56. al-Tabari related it in his History: 2/128–139, by way of Ibn Ishaq.]

al-Waqidi said: As for Mahmud, the elephant of the Negus, it crouched down and did not advance upon the Haram, so it was saved. The other elephant advanced and was pelted with stones. [Manuscript "B" reads: "did not advance" as "yashja'" ("was brave").]

Muqatil ibn Sulayman claimed that the cause which emboldened the companions of the elephant was that some young men of Quraysh went out as merchants to the land of the Negus. They drew near the seashore, and there was a church (bay'ah) of the Christians which Quraysh called "al-Haykal." They camped there, lit a fire and roasted food. When they departed, they left the fire as it was on a windy day. The wind blew, and the Haykal caught fire and blazed. The news (al-sarikh) went to the Negus, who was enraged for the sake of the church, so he sent Abraha to demolish the Kaʿbah.

And he said in it: At that time in Mecca there was Abu Mas'ud al-Thaqafi, who was blind. He would spend the summer in al-Ta'if and the winter in Mecca. He was a discerning and noble man, through whose opinion affairs were set right, and he was a close friend of Abd al-Muttalib. Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "What do you have to offer? This is a day in which one cannot do without your opinion." Abu Mas'ud said: "Take us up to Hira'." So he went up the mountain. Abu Mas'ud said to Abd al-Muttalib: "Go to a hundred camels, dedicate them to God, mark them with sandals, and then release them in the Sacred Precinct. Perhaps some of these black men will slaughter some of them, and then the Lord of this House will become angry and take them." Abd al-Muttalib did this. The people went to those camels, mounted them, and slaughtered some of them. Abd al-Muttalib began to supplicate. Abu Mas'ud said: "Indeed this House has a Lord who protects it. Tubba', king of Yemen, descended upon the courtyard of this House intending to demolish it, but God prevented him and afflicted him, and darkness fell upon him for three days. When Tubba' saw this, he clothed the House in white Qibati cloth, honored it, and slaughtered a camel for it."

[Then Abu Mas'ud said] Look toward the sea. Abd al-Muttalib looked and said: "I see a white bird rising from the seashore." He said: "Fix your gaze on it; where does it settle?" He said: "I see it has circled above our heads." He said: "Do you recognize it?" He said: "By God, I do not recognize it. It is neither Najdi, nor Tihami, nor western, nor Syrian." He said: "What is its shape?" He said: "It resembles locusts [al-Ya'asib], with pebbles in its beak, as if they were pebbles of the hadhf (sling). It has come like the night, one of them chasing another. In front of every flock there is a bird leading it, red-beaked, black-headed, long-necked. It came until it passed over the army of the people [and it approached] [and it struck] above their heads. When all the men had gathered, the birds let fall what was in their beaks upon those beneath them, with the name of its owner written on every stone. Then they turned back and departed from whence they had come." When morning came, the two descended from the peak of the mountain and walked a hillock, but they found no one. Then they approached another hillock but heard no sound. They said: "The people spent the night awake [sahirin]," [in B: samidin], "and in the morning they are asleep." When they drew near the army of the people, behold, they were dead and still. The stone would fall upon the helmet [bayda] of one of them, which is what is worn on the head for protection in battle, and tear through it until it reached his brain; it would pierce the elephant and the beast, and the stone would sink into the ground from the force of its impact. Abd al-Muttalib then took an axe from their axes and dug until he went deep into the earth, and filled it with their wealth of red gold and jewels. He dug a pit for his companion and filled it likewise. Then he said to Abu Mas'ud: "Come, choose: if you wish, my pit, and if you wish, your pit, and if you wish, both are yours together." Abu Mas'ud said: "Choose for me over yourself." Abd al-Muttalib said: "I have not failed to place the finest goods in my pit, so it is yours." Each of them sat by his own pit. Abd al-Muttalib called out among the people, and they returned and took from their surplus until they were overwhelmed by it. Through this, Abd al-Muttalib became the leader of Quraysh, and they granted him authority. Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Mas'ud remained in their families, in wealth from that money, and God defended His Ka'bah and His House.

They differed about the date of the Year of the Elephant. Muqatil said: it was forty years before the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ).
Al-Kalbi said: twenty-three years before.
Most scholars hold that it occurred in the year in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was born.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ Muqatil said: there was one elephant with them. Al-Dahhak said: there were eight elephants. It was also said twelve, apart from the greatest elephant. It is singular because He attributed them to the greatest elephant. It was also said: for the harmony of the verse endings.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 105, verse 2–3:

﴿Did He not make their scheme into misguidance?﴾ "Kaydahum" means their deceit and their effort to destroy the Ka'bah. His words ﴿into misguidance﴾ mean (they were led) astray from what they intended, and He caused their scheme to go astray, so that they did not reach the Ka'bah nor what they had hoped to achieve by their scheme. Muqatil said: "in loss." It was also said: "in nullification."

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ many, scattered, following one another. It was said: they were herds like the herded camels (ibil mu'abbalah). Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Ababil" means groups in dispersal; it is said: "The horses came ababil from here and there."

Al-Farra' said: "It has no singular from its own form." It was also said: its singular is ibalah (إبالة). Al-Kisa'i said: "I used to hear the grammarians say: its singular is abul (أبول), like 'ajul and 'ajajil" [[Al-Farra' mentioned the phrase in the previous passage as follows: "Some grammarians, namely al-Kisa'i, said: I used to hear the grammarians say: abuk is like al-'ujul and al-'ajajil."]].

It was also said: its singular is from its own form, ibbil (إبِّيلٌ).

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were birds that had beaks like the beaks of birds and talons like the paws of dogs [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/297. As-Suyuti in ad-Durr al-Manthur (8/630) added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in ad-Dala'il.]].

And 'Ikrimah said: they had heads like the heads of beasts of prey. Al-Rabi' said: they had fangs like the fangs of beasts of prey.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they were green, with yellow beaks. Qatadah said: they were black birds that came from the direction of the sea, in groups after groups, and with each bird were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, which would shatter whatever they struck.

And 'Ikrimah said: they had heads like the heads of beasts of prey. Al-Rabi' said: they had fangs like the fangs of beasts of prey.

﴿They pelted them with stones of sijjil﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: the birds shrieked and pelted them with the stones, then Allah sent a wind which struck the stones and increased their force, so that no stone fell upon a man without coming out from his other side, and if it fell upon his head, it came out from his anus.

﴿So He made them like eaten straw﴾: like crops and chaff that animals have eaten and passed as dung, so it dried up and its parts scattered. He likened the severing of their joints to the scattering of the parts of dung. Mujahid said: "al-'asf" is the leaf of wheat. Qatadah said: it is chaff. 'Ikrimah said: like the grain when it has been eaten and has become hollow. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the outer husk that surrounds the wheat grain, in the shape of a covering for it.
